question: Can I still add urea to my rice when it has started producing?
minimum_context_answer:
If the rice has already formed heads (panicles) and you can see flowering or grains starting to fill, do not add urea now. At this stage the crop has taken up most of the nitrogen it needs, so late urea gives little or no yield benefit and can instead cause lodging, increase disease and pest pressure, and delay maturity.

The only time a final nitrogen dose helps is just before the head emerges—at panicle initiation/early booting—when the panicle is still inside the stem and not yet visible. If your crop is already “producing” in the sense that heads are out or grains are forming, it’s too late for urea.

For future crops, plan urea in splits: a basal dose at planting/transplanting, another during active tillering, and the last at panicle initiation. Avoid applying nitrogen after heading.
agricultural_chatbot_answer:
You can still add urea if your rice is at panicle initiation or booting and the heads are just about to emerge, but once most panicles have come out and flowering/grain filling has begun, it’s better not to. A small nitrogen dose at booting can help grain number and size; after flowering it won’t increase yield, and it can cause lodging, more disease/insect pressure, and delay maturity.

A quick way to decide: feel the top stem (the flag leaf sheath). If the panicle is still inside (booting) or only just emerging and you don’t yet see open flowers, you’re in the last useful window for a light topdress. If most heads are out and you can see flowering or small grains, skip the urea.

If you are still within that window and the crop looks a bit pale or thin, apply a light topdress—about one 50‑kg bag of urea per hectare (roughly half a bag per acre). Do not exceed this at this stage. How you apply matters:
- In lowland/flooded rice: apply when the water is shallow or after briefly draining; broadcast in the cool of the day and re-flood lightly after a day or so. Avoid spreading onto deep standing water at midday to reduce losses.
- In upland/non-flooded rice: place or lightly incorporate urea a little away from the plant base and cover it; apply just before a light rain or irrigate so it dissolves into the root zone. Avoid placing granules on wet leaves.

With your sandy loam soil and the generally dry seasonal outlook, only apply if you can ensure some moisture from irrigation or imminent light rain; otherwise the urea can be lost and won’t pay back. Also, avoid putting it down right before a heavy storm that could wash it away.

If the crop has already flowered and is filling grain, don’t add granular urea now. Focus instead on steady water management, weed and pest control, and plan to improve nitrogen management next crop by splitting nitrogen earlier (basal, active tillering, and panicle initiation) and building soil organic matter with compost/manure and residue retention so the crop has enough nitrogen before this late stage.
